deep.reconstruction:
This page continues §VI, which hopes that experiments and theory will give the stiffness of any column. Euler says that once the stiffness is known as a function of material, width and thickness, it could be assigned point by point even for a column of variable section.

§VII states the constitutive principle of the whole theory. The bending moment of the external force about a cross-section is M = Pf, and the column's 'moment de roideur' (flexural rigidity, modern EI) is Ekk. The radius of curvature produced there is then r = Ekk/(Pf); equivalently, the moment needed to produce curvature 1/r is Ekk/r. This is the Bernoulli–Euler moment–curvature law M = EI·κ.

Euler adds two remarks:
- Ekk has the dimensions of a force times the square of a length, 'semblable aux expressions qui marquent le moment d'inertie des corps'.
- For flexure alone it does not matter whether the body recovers after the load is removed. 'Elasticity' in the sense of restitution therefore plays no role; the same theory covers elastic and merely stiff ('roides') bodies.

§VIII uses the principle to justify the experimental rule of §IV. The column is clamped vertically at the base A and loaded at the top C by a small horizontal force F, with AC = a. Coordinates are BP = x along the axis and PM = y, the small lateral deflection. For small deflection the radius of curvature is dx²/ddy, with dx held constant. The moment at M is F(a−x).

On the next page this gives ddy/dx² = F(a−x)/Ekk. Two integrations with y = y' = 0 at the clamped end give y = F(3ax² − x³)/(6Ekk). The tip deflection is therefore Dδ = Fa³/(3Ekk), so Ekk = F·AC³/(3Dδ). This is the standard linear cantilever result, and it serves as the static test for measuring stiffness before the buckling analysis that follows.
errors: No real error. The curvature is linearized (1/r ≈ y''), which Euler himself flags: the rule holds only when Dδ is very small compared with AC.

The meaning of 'Ekk' is left loose. Euler attributes the dimension force×length² to the product as a whole and does not separate a material modulus from a geometric second moment of the section. On the previous page he only guesses the dependence on thickness (square, cube or fourth power).

ideas.what: Radius of curvature = rigidity / bending moment (r = Ekk/Pf); moment needed for curvature 1/r is Ekk/r
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Bernoulli moment–curvature law M = EI κ
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jakob Bernoulli (1694/1705); Daniel Bernoulli; Euler (Methodus inveniendi, 1744, Additamentum I)
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi (1744), Additamentum I 'De curvis elasticis'; also later column papers

ideas.what: Flexural stiffness has dimensions force × length² and is likened to the moment of inertia of bodies
ideas.modern_name: Analogy behind calling the second moment of area I the 'area moment of inertia'
ideas.usually_credited_to: Terminology developed in 19th-century strength of materials (Navier and successors); unsure of the precise first user
ideas.where_published: This paper (E238); Truesdell's 1960 account of Euler's elastica and column work discusses E238

ideas.what: Flexure theory needs only stiffness, not restitution: it applies equally to elastic and merely stiff ('roides') bodies
ideas.modern_name: Bending theory as a constitutive moment–curvature relation, independent of whether the response is reversible
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Bernoulli/Euler; discussed by Truesdell

ideas.what: Small-deflection cantilever with end load: Dδ = Fa³/(3EI), used to measure EI experimentally
ideas.modern_name: Cantilever tip deflection formula / static stiffness test
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1744 and here); standard engineering result

ideas.what: Assigning a local rigidity to columns of variable thickness
ideas.modern_name: Beams and columns of variable cross-section (non-uniform EI)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, later papers on columns (1770s); Lagrange (1770–73)
ideas.where_published: Euler's later column papers on variable cross-section (exact Eneström numbers unsure)

deep.surprise_reason: The page restates Euler's well-known 1744 moment–curvature principle and sets up the standard cantilever formula. The remark linking rigidity to moments of inertia, and the one on elastic versus stiff bodies, are interesting but are covered in Truesdell's treatment of E238. The variable-section thread was taken up by Euler himself and by Lagrange.
